newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Pressure on Mobutu rises after Kisangani's fall.
newsitem.headline: Pressure on Mobutu rises after Kisangani's fall.

text.p: Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko's prospects of holding onto power in Zaire looked significantly weaker on Monday two days after rebels seized the key city of Kisangani.
The rebels were exultant after their biggest victory yet in their five-month war to oust Mobutu. They were in full control of Kisangani where they were welcomed as liberators.
But further away in France, the man they want to topple and whose army has lost the third largest city, was admitted to a hospital for further cancer treatment.
"It is only treatment and the president is well," a spokesman at Mobutu's French Riviera villa told Reuters by telephone.
He said the condition of Mobutu, who has ruled Africa's third largest country for 32 years, was "no cause for concern".

The veteran ruler, blamed by the opposition and the rebels for ruining Africa's potentially richest country, has spent much of his time at his luxury home in Roquebrune-Cap Martin since he underwent prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland last August.
He came back to France on February 21 and had been due to return to Zaire last week, according to his son and spokesman, but his departure was delayed, apparently for medical reasons.
The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), led by Laurent Kabila, has now overrun about one fifth of Zaire.

Kisangani is 1,200 km (750 miles) from Kinshasa, Zaire's capital, and in geographic terms the Mobutu government still has the upper hand. But the future seemed increasingly bleak for the ailing president and his supporters.
The rebels, commanded by Kabila's 25-year-old son Joseph, were warmly greeted by many Kisangani residents when they entered the city.
Mobutu's army has always failed to hold its ground since Kabila launched his rebellion on Zaire's eastern border last October.

Kisangani, the army's eastern headquarters until soldiers fled after a looting spree, was no exception. The government recruited some foreign mercenaries, believed to be mostly Bosnian Serbs, to try to put some backbone into the demoralised troops.
Joseph Kabila, operational commander for the rebels' northern sector, told Reuters in Kisangani he believed most of the mercenaries flew out of the city on Friday night.
Civilian support for his father Laurent is not restricted to areas now controlled by the veteran former Marxist.
"His army is an army of liberation and he must free us from the dictatorship of Mobutu," opposition militant Jose Wasunde, 34, told Reuters in Kinshasa.

The rebels say their next target is Lubumbashi, capital of the mineral-rich Shaba region whose copper, cobalt and precious metals should make Zaire a well-off country instead of one of the poorest in the world.
The capture of Kisangani complicated international mediation efforts. The rebels say they will not agree a ceasefire before negotiations and they insist talks must centre on Mobutu's departure.
It was also another disaster for the 370,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees stranded in eastern Zaire who have trekked ahead of the rebel advance for the past five months.

They are the rump of the Hutus who fled in fear of retaliation for the genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994. Their defeated army has fought with Zaire's troops against Kabila's rebels, who include many ethnic Tutsis.

Relief workers plan to start repatriating Rwandan Hutu refugees from Zaire's once teeming Tingi Tingi camp on Monday but they say prospects for those driven further west by a relentless rebel advance look bleak.
Tingi Tingi, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani, housed 170,000 refugees before most fled the rebel advance. Only the weak or sick -- about 1,000 people -- stayed behind.
As many as 150,000 Hutus were in Ubundu, clustered on the banks of the Zaire River 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani. Perthius said as many more were missing in the jungle.
